questions.q: What does "blameless" actually mean in a blameless postmortem, according to this lesson?
options: Nobody is ever held accountable for any decision made during the incident
The investigation assumes individuals acted reasonably given the information and tools they had, and asks why the system allowed a bad outcome
The postmortem document is deleted after the meeting so no record of mistakes exists
Only managers are allowed to attend, so individual contributors can't be blamed in the room
questions.explain: Blameless doesn't mean consequence-free or mistake-free — it means the process assumes reasonable intent and investigates systemic causes, which gets people to speak honestly and produces a more accurate timeline.

questions.q: Which section of a postmortem document is pulled directly from the Scribe's real-time log kept during the incident?
options: The timeline
The "what went well" section
The action items section
The summary
questions.explain: The timeline section reconstructs detection, declaration, key decisions, mitigation, and closure using the actual timestamped record kept live during the incident, not memory after the fact.

questions.q: In the Five Whys example about a bad config deploy, where did the chain of questioning actually land?
options: On the specific engineer who typed the bad config value, recommending they be retrained
On a process gap — config schema changes never triggered a validation review — rather than on an individual mistake
On the monitoring tool, concluding it should be replaced entirely
On the original deploy itself, with no further explanation needed
questions.explain: Five Whys is meant to move past the shallow first answer (a bad config value) to a fixable, systemic cause: validation never checked ranges because schema changes didn't trigger a review.

questions.q: What three things does this lesson say an action item needs before it's actually worth writing down?
options: A severity label, a Scribe, and a Communications Lead
A vague description, team-wide ownership, and no deadline
A specific owner, a due date, and a concrete definition of done
A root cause section, a timeline, and an impact estimate
questions.explain: Vague, unowned, undated action items are where good postmortems stall — a specific person, a deadline, and a clear definition of done make an item actually trackable to closure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a postmortem with great root-cause analysis but zero completed action items hasn't actually accomplished much?
options: Because postmortem documents expire automatically after 30 days
Because root-cause analysis is considered optional in most incident programs
Because action items are only useful if the incident was a SEV1
Because without tracking fixes to actual completion, the same incident will, with mechanical certainty, happen again
questions.explain: Documenting a problem without following through to a completed fix leaves the underlying system condition unchanged, so the same failure mode remains available to recur.
